prose:
# Iran turns away Pakistan's mediator, and oil tops $110

Iran told Pakistan's mediator that it will not negotiate until Washington moves first. Iran's mines and drones now reach tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude, the world's main oil price, is back above $110 a barrel. One pattern runs through the day's events: whoever controls something that others need uses it to bargain. Iran controls a sea lane. Washington controls the missile warnings, Patriot missiles and satellite links that Ukraine depends on, and Kyiv says Washington used them to apply pressure. Governments in France and Italy answer street anger with police and soldiers. Brazil's government times fuel subsidies and welfare payments around a close vote. The people with the least control pay the most: drivers, families who heat their homes, and Ukrainian civilians. The AI trade shows a similar shift of risk. In Seoul, Korean small investors bought the chip shares that foreign investors sold, and the losses now fall on them.

## Iran spreads its attacks on tankers beyond Hormuz

The war began on Feb. 28, when US and Israeli strikes killed Iran's Supreme Leader Khamenei. Iran answered with missiles and drones across the region and shut Hormuz. Before the war, about a fifth of the world's oil went through Hormuz. Pakistan brokered a ceasefire in April and a 14-point memorandum in June. The memorandum failed within weeks, and the ceasefire ended by early July. On Oct. 20 Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, flew to Tehran to revive it. He left the next day with nothing. Iran's leaders told him that talks will start only after the US meets their conditions. These include an end to the US naval blockade of Iranian ports and the release of Iran's frozen money. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said that not one gram of Iran's enriched uranium will leave the country. Iran holds about 440 kilograms enriched to 60%, and Washington wants that uranium out first. A Qatari team came after Munir and left after about 30 minutes. Foreign Minister Araghchi said that Hormuz stays restricted until the US honours the June memorandum.

Each side wants the other to move first, so the mediators have nothing to carry. Meanwhile, Iran bargains with shipping. It declared Hormuz closed on Oct. 17. On Oct. 20 a supertanker hit a mine south of Hormuz and caught fire. The Revolutionary Guard says that the ship broke Iranian rules. It also claims that two tankers burned and that it shot down a US drone. The US Navy says it stopped Iran's attempts to hit ships, and Washington says Hormuz is open. The ship-tracking firm Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on ships in two weeks, about twice its count of a few days earlier. Analysts at LSEG say the strikes now reach the Gulf of Oman. That is the important change. After the war began, Gulf producers sent more oil around Hormuz. Pipelines carry crude to ports outside it, and tankers move cargo from ship to ship in the Gulf of Oman. Earlier Kpler data showed about 40% of Gulf crude on pipelines that bypass Hormuz, against 17% before the war. Attacks outside Hormuz put that workaround in danger.

Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen press on another part of the workaround. Saudi Arabia now pipes crude across the desert to Yanbu, its export port on the Red Sea. On Oct. 19 the Houthis claimed hits on Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and the airports of Riyadh and Abha. Saudi Arabia confirmed none of these hits, and Reuters could not verify them. Saudi Arabia confirmed only that its forces shot down a ballistic missile and a drone over Riyadh on Oct. 20. Its partners send help, but only for defence. Britain sends Typhoon fighters that will not strike Yemen. Turkey's government sent a mutual-defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to its parliament. The US does not strike the Houthis itself.

Brent touched $111.99 on Oct. 20, its highest in five months. It fell to about $107 on unconfirmed reports of a US-Iran breakthrough, and it went back above $110 after Iran's answer to Munir. Nobody agrees how much Gulf oil still moves. Energy Secretary Chris Wright says about 80% of the pre-war flow. The International Energy Agency put September exports just over 75% of the pre-war level. Commerzbank's Carsten Fritsch, citing Kpler, says the seven-day average fell to 8.5 million barrels a day, from more than 20 million the week before. All three figures can be true. The first two are averages over weeks, mostly before the October attacks. The third covers one week at the peak of the attacks. Goldman Sachs puts the war premium in the price at nearly $25 a barrel. It sees $120 if the attacks grow, and $80 if Gulf exports return to normal. The US emergency oil reserve is at a 44-year low after months of releases, so Washington has less oil to soften a new shock.

The same waters carry gas. Qatar moves its gas from ship to ship in the Gulf of Oman to get it past Hormuz. Kpler expects Qatar to ship about 0.6 million tonnes of gas in October, against 1.6 million in September, and it ties the drop to the attacks. Europe's wholesale gas price passed 88 euros a megawatt-hour on Oct. 19, its highest since December 2022. On Oct. 21 the EU's gas stores were 74.6% full, against a 90% target, as the heating season starts.

People far apart pay for this. Tanker crews sail through mined water. People in Riyadh and Abha live under missile alerts, and a Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people on Oct. 10. In Yemen, the UN counts more than 250,000 people displaced since Aug. 1. A Houthi missile killed between 53 and 73 recruits at a training camp in Shabwa on Oct. 19. Iranians live under the blockade, and their country's money stays frozen. Buyers of diesel and heating gas everywhere pay for the risk, and the US Energy Department already works with refiners on a diesel shortage.

There is a serious case that this is hard bargaining, not collapse. Iran published its conditions on Sept. 20, so Munir heard nothing new. Hard public lines also came before the April ceasefire and the June memorandum. Trump says the war will end soon, and the US holds midterm elections on Nov. 3. In April a ceasefire announcement cut Brent by about 14% in one day. Treasury Secretary Bessent predicts oil at $40 to $50 once the war ends. A hurricane also cut Gulf of Mexico output for three weeks, so part of this week's rise is American. On that reading, the war premium can disappear in a single day. Today, though, the only working channel came back empty, and Iran ties Hormuz to a first move by Washington.

## Witkoff takes the Oslo plan for Ukraine to Putin

Before this week, relations between Washington and Kyiv were at their worst since the winter of 2025, by the Wall Street Journal's account. Trump wants Ukraine to stop its drone strikes on Russian refineries, because he blames them for high diesel prices. Washington asked Kyiv six times to stop. On Oct. 16 Trump waived nearly all the penalties in the Graham Act, the Russia sanctions law that he signed in September. The waiver has no end date. Kyiv says that Washington then cut or slowed three things: warnings of Russian ballistic missiles, Patriot missiles that European allies paid for, and Starshield, the military satellite service that Ukraine's drones use. Secretary of State Rubio denies that the US held back anything on purpose. On Oct. 20 in Oslo, Zelensky met Trump's envoy, Steve Witkoff. The leaders of Norway and Finland took part, with officials from the big European powers, the EU and NATO. Ukraine joined a US-European plan for Putin, and Zelensky says the missile warnings work again. On Oct. 21 Witkoff took the Oslo plan to Putin in St. Petersburg.

## Super Micro and SpaceX beat forecasts, and Seoul rebounds

For most of October, investors sold the companies that supply AI hardware. They doubted that the big buyers can keep paying. Citadel's founder, Ken Griffin, said that AI is in a bubble, and Ray Dalio agreed. Gartner projects about $7 trillion of AI spending against $3.6 trillion of AI revenue by 2030. Korea's main stock index, the KOSPI, fell 3.73% on Oct. 20 and closed about 17% below its level at the start of the month. That day, the Korean AI data-centre company Elice closed about 32% below its offer price on its first day of trading. Small investors who bought in the offering lost about a third of their money. In Taiwan, foreign investors sold shares for a tenth day in a row.

## France and Italy send in soldiers before Saturday's protests

France's unrest began in September with school blockades over missing teachers and decaying buildings. Diesel at about 2.35 euros a litre and a plan to cut 54 billion euros from next year's budget then joined the anger. On Saturday, Oct. 17, a leaderless online call brought students, former Yellow Vests and union members onto the streets together. The Interior Ministry counted about 550,000 marchers, and the CGT union counted more than 800,000. Most marched in peace, but riots and looting followed in many cities. Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin says police took more than 2,500 people into custody by Oct. 19. Courts jail even first offenders: three looters in Lille got ten months each. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez puts the number of injured police, gendarmes and firefighters near 1,000. A protester died of cardiac and respiratory arrest in Paris, and investigators still examine the cause. Grenades maimed two 17-year-olds: a boy in Saint-Etienne lost a hand, and a girl in Mulhouse lost an eye. Parliament opened an inquiry into police conduct. Bloomberg estimates the total damage at 10 to 12 billion euros.

[Will Saturday's protests in France draw less than half last week's crowd? UBIK puts it at 80 percent.](/forecasts/q_20261020_04)

## Lula and Bolsonaro take their runoff fight to court

Brazil votes on Sunday, Oct. 25. In the first round on Oct. 4, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro took 47.03% of valid votes and President Lula took 45.16%, although the polls expected Lula to lead. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who serves a 27-year sentence for a coup plot after the 2022 election. The son pledged to free his father. After the first round the gap narrowed, and every poll published on Oct. 20 sits within its margin of error. Datafolha and Quaest give Bolsonaro 51% to 49% of valid votes. Vox Brasil shows Lula ahead for the first time, 46.4% to 44.6%. Part of the spread comes from method: some polls count only valid votes, and others count everyone they asked.

forecasts.resolution_source: French Interior Ministry national count of demonstrators for Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, as published by the ministry or relayed from it by AFP, Le Monde or franceinfo
forecasts.resolution_rule: Yes if the Interior Ministry's nationwide count of protesters in France for Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, is below 275,000, which is half its count of 550,000 for Oct. 17. No if it is 275,000 or more. Use the latest full-day national figure the ministry publishes by 23:59 Paris time on Oct. 31, 2026; if it publishes only an intraday figure, use the latest one published by then. Ignore later revisions and any count by unions, organizers or independent counters. If the ministry publishes a national figure for Oct. 24, that figure settles the question whatever else happens. If it publishes none by the deadline: void if the national protest day was moved from Oct. 24 to a later date; otherwise Yes, including when the calls are withdrawn or banned or the protests are too scattered for a national count.

methodology.thesis: Iran will not negotiate until Washington moves first, and its attacks now reach the routes that take Gulf oil and gas around Hormuz. That risk keeps Brent above $110 and Europe's gas price at its highest level since 2022. The cost travels far from the Gulf. Washington presses Kyiv to stop refinery strikes that push up diesel prices, and it controls the missile warnings, Patriot missiles and satellite links that Ukraine needs. France and Italy answer anger over living costs with soldiers, curfews and new penalties, because their budgets leave little room for concessions. Brazil keeps fuel cheap through a tied runoff with money from a crude export tax that stays while Brent is above $100. In Asia, strong results from AI suppliers lifted chip stocks, but the October slide already moved losses from foreign investors to Korean households. In each case, the side that controls something others depend on uses it to bargain, and people with little control carry the cost.

currents.title: Iran war: talks stall as Gulf attacks push oil above $110
currents.mechanism: Iran is using Gulf shipping as its bargaining chip: it keeps Hormuz restricted, and mines and strikes tankers in and now beyond the strait, until Washington meets its terms, while its Houthi allies fire at the Saudi oil sites and cities behind the main route around the strait. Each attack shrinks or endangers the oil that can leave the Gulf, and that risk, more than any measured shortfall, holds Brent above $110; Goldman puts the war premium near $25 a barrel, which would deflate if exports normalised or talks resumed.

developments.title: Iran sends Pakistan's mediator home empty-handed: no talks until the US meets its conditions, and the uranium stays
developments.what_happened: Prior situation: the war began on 28 February 2026, when US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Khamenei; Iran answered with missiles and drones across the region and shut the Strait of Hormuz. Pakistan brokered a two-week ceasefire on 8 April; talks in Islamabad on 11-12 April failed and the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports. On 17 June both sides signed the Islamabad memorandum: 14 points, an immediate halt to military operations, 60 days to negotiate a final deal, phased US sanctions relief and lifting of the blockade, and Iranian guarantees of safe passage through Hormuz plus a renewed pledge not to seek nuclear weapons. It unravelled within weeks: on 26 June a Revolutionary Guard drone hit a Singapore-flagged ship in the strait, the US struck about ten Iranian targets around Hormuz, and the ceasefire was over by 8 July. On 20 September Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei set out seven conditions that Washington must meet before talks, among them ending the war on all fronts, releasing frozen Iranian funds, lifting the naval blockade, halting attacks on Iranian territory and ending interference in Iran's internal affairs; Washington in turn has demanded Iran hand over its highly enriched uranium. New: Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, arrived in Tehran on 20 October to revive the memorandum and met President Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf and Rezaei. He left on 21 October without a concession. Iran told him negotiations would not begin until its conditions were met; Rezaei said not one gram of Iran's enriched uranium, about 440 kg enriched to 60%, would leave the country, calling it national wealth; Ghalibaf reportedly said Iran had nothing new to tell Washington. A senior Qatari delegation arrived after Munir and left after about 30 minutes without a breakthrough. On 21 October Foreign Minister Araghchi told Iraq's Al-Ikhbariya that Hormuz stays restricted until the US fulfils the Islamabad memorand
developments.why_it_matters: The only active channel to end the war, Pakistan with Qatar behind it, came back with nothing, and Iran has tied the reopening of Hormuz to Washington moving first. That removes the near-term exit the oil market briefly priced on 20 October and leaves the uranium stockpile, the core US demand, explicitly off the table.
developments.plain_summary: Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, flew to Tehran this week to try to restart peace talks between Iran and the United States, and left with nothing. Iran's leaders told him they will not even sit down with Washington until the US first meets their conditions, including ending the war on every front, releasing Iran's frozen money and lifting the US Navy's blockade of Iranian ports. They also said none of Iran's roughly 440 kilos of highly enriched uranium will leave the country, which is exactly what Washington wants. A Qatari team that followed was gone in about half an hour. And Iran's foreign minister said shipping through the Strait of Hormuz stays restricted until the US honours the deal Pakistan brokered in June, which fell apart within weeks.

developments.title: Mines and strikes on tankers spread south of Hormuz into the Gulf of Oman
developments.what_happened: Iran declared Hormuz closed on 17 October and the Revolutionary Guard formally barred ships of all nations on 18 October; the US says the strait is open and that it controls it (Central Command counted more than 40 ships through in 24 hours around 16 October). On 20 October a supertanker caught fire after hitting a sea mine south of the strait; the Guard's navy said the ship had violated Iranian regulations and claimed two tankers were set ablaze and a US MQ-9 drone shot down. US Navy Capt. Nicholas Delio said Iranian attempts to target ships were thwarted. Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on vessels in the past two weeks, up from 9-11 reported days earlier; LSEG analysts say the strikes now reach beyond the strait into the Gulf of Oman, threatening ship-to-ship transfers and loadings there. Kpler counted only 7 vessels through Hormuz on 8 October, the lowest in over two months, against more than 125 large vessels a day before the war. Iran's first vice president, Mohammad Reza Aref, said on 19 October that Iran has no choice but to assert control of the strait and that the US must pay the price.
developments.why_it_matters: Since the war, Gulf producers have kept oil flowing partly by piping it around Hormuz and loading or transferring it outside the strait. Attacks in the Gulf of Oman threaten that workaround, not just the strait itself.
developments.plain_summary: The fight over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war, is getting worse. Iran declared the strait closed last weekend. On Tuesday a supertanker hit a mine just south of it and caught fire; Iran's Revolutionary Guard said the ship had broken Iranian rules. The ship-tracking firm Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on ships in two weeks, double the count of a few days earlier, and analysts say the strikes now reach into the Gulf of Oman, outside the strait, where tankers load and swap cargoes. The US Navy says the strait is open and that it stopped Iranian attempts to hit ships.

developments.title: Houthis claim hits on Aramco's Yanbu and Shaybah and two airports; Saudi Arabia confirms only an interception over Riyadh
developments.what_happened: Prior situation: the Houthis' war with Saudi Arabia, dormant for about four years, restarted on 13 July 2026 after Saudi-led coalition forces stopped a Houthi delegation landing at Sanaa airport; since then the group has hit Saudi oil sites and airports almost daily. A 10 October strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, closed the airport and led Saudi Arabia to postpone its flagship investment conference to 2027. New: on 19 October the Houthis claimed attacks on an Aramco site at Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield, King Khalid airport and Abha airport. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed any of those, and Reuters could not verify them; from the latest wave Saudi Arabia had earlier confirmed only that something fell on the border city of Najran. On 20 October coalition spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said a ballistic missile and a drone aimed at Riyadh were intercepted and the launch platform destroyed; AFP heard two explosions before civil defence lifted the alert. Araghchi said Iran's offer to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has had no answer. Inside Yemen, a Houthi missile strike on a training camp in Shabwa on 19 October killed between 53 and 73 recruits by differing counts.
developments.why_it_matters: Yanbu, on the Red Sea, is where Saudi Arabia ships the crude it pipes across the country to avoid Hormuz, and Shaybah is a major oilfield. A credible threat to them is a threat to the main bypass that has kept Gulf oil reaching the market.
developments.plain_summary: Yemen's Houthis, who are backed by Iran, have been firing at Saudi Arabia almost every day since their war with the kingdom restarted in July. On Monday they claimed hits on two Saudi oil sites, the Red Sea export hub at Yanbu and the Shaybah oilfield, and on the airports in Riyadh and Abha. Saudi Arabia hasn't confirmed any of that. What it has confirmed is that on Tuesday its forces shot down a ballistic missile and a drone aimed at Riyadh; residents heard two blasts. Yanbu matters well beyond Saudi Arabia: it is where the kingdom ships the oil it now pipes across the desert to get around Hormuz.

developments.title: Britain sends defensive-only jets to Saudi Arabia; Turkey sends the Mecca defence pact to parliament
developments.what_happened: On 20 October Britain announced it is deploying RAF Typhoon fighters to Saudi Arabia to shoot down Houthi drones and missiles, with an A400M transport plane, military advisers and a further 90 days of air-to-air refuelling support. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the jets will fly defensive missions only and will not strike the Houthis in Yemen. He discussed the move with Hegseth at the Pentagon; the US has declined to launch offensive strikes of its own. Saudi Arabia has also sought air-defence help from France, Pakistan and Egypt. The same day Turkey's government sent the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement to parliament for ratification. Signed on 7 August by Erdogan, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif, its Article 2 treats an attack on one as an attack on all three; it requires Pakistani forces in Saudi Arabia for at least ten years, bars withdrawal for a decade, and sets up a secretariat in Riyadh. It takes effect only after all three countries ratify. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Turkey will not send soldiers abroad to attack, and Turkey needs a separate parliamentary vote for any troop deployment; committee debate could start as early as Friday. Egypt's parliament is due to vote on 26 October on letting Sisi send troops to defend Saudi Arabia.
developments.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia is building a coalition to defend its cities and oil, but every partner is drawing a line at defence. That raises the cost of Houthi attacks without widening the war into Yemen.
developments.plain_summary: Countries are lining up to help protect Saudi Arabia, but carefully. Britain is sending Typhoon fighter jets to shoot down Houthi drones and missiles and says they will not strike the Houthis in Yemen. Turkey's government sent parliament a defence pact signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August, under which an attack on one counts as an attack on all three. It takes effect only once all three ratify it, and Turkey says it won't send troops to fight abroad without a separate vote. The US, meanwhile, has declined to strike the Houthis itself.

developments.title: Brent tops $110 as estimates of how much Gulf oil is moving diverge
developments.what_happened: Brent touched $111.99 on 20 October, a five-month high, fell about 3% to near $107 on unconfirmed reports of a US-Iran breakthrough, and was back above $110 on 21 October after Iran's answer to Munir. US crude (WTI) was around $99 for December delivery and near $104 for November. Brent first topped $110 since May on 16 October, and is up roughly 70-80% this year; by one tally it peaked around $138 on 7 April, the eve of the ceasefire. The physical Brent spot price published by the US Energy Information Administration was $126.55 on 14 October, about $20 or more above the futures price quoted in the news. The flow figures conflict: Energy Secretary Chris Wright says Gulf supply is back to about 80% of pre-war levels; the IEA put September Gulf crude exports at 13.9 million barrels a day, just over 75% of pre-war; Kpler and Vortexa data showed Middle East crude exports in September above pre-war levels, led by Saudi Arabia; but Commerzbank's Carsten Fritsch, citing Kpler, said the seven-day average of Gulf crude exports fell to 8.5 million barrels a day from more than 20 million the week before. Earlier Kpler data had Hormuz itself carrying about 10.1 million barrels a day in September against 13.6 million before the war, with about 40% of Gulf crude now leaving by pipelines that bypass the strait, against 17% before. Goldman Sachs estimates a war premium of nearly $25 a barrel in the price, forecasts $90 Brent in December and $80 on average in 2027, and sees $120 if attacks intensify or $80 if Gulf exports normalise. The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at a 44-year low after months of emergency releases.
developments.why_it_matters: The price is being set less by a measured shortfall than by the risk that the routes still working get cut. The figures can be reconciled: Wright's and the IEA's are averages over weeks or a month that mostly predate the October attack wave and count oil piped around Hormuz, while Kpler's 8.5 million is a one-week snapshot taken as attacks peaked, and seven-day averages swing by millions of barrels on a few supertanker loadings.
developments.plain_summary: Brent crude, the world's main oil price, rose above $110 a barrel, its highest in five months, and the American benchmark is near $100. The odd thing is that nobody agrees how much Gulf oil is actually getting out. The US energy secretary says about 80 percent of the pre-war flow. The International Energy Agency put September at a bit over three quarters. But tanker tracking from Kpler showed last week's average plunging to 8.5 million barrels a day from more than 20 million the week before. Goldman Sachs reckons about $25 of today's price is fear of what comes next: oil could hit $120 if the attacks intensify, or drop to $80 if Gulf exports get back to normal.

developments.title: Italy's power and gas bills jump as the heating goes on, and Rome's gas cap waits for 2027
developments.what_happened: Italy's energy regulator ARERA raised the electricity price for about 3 million vulnerable households by 37.3% for October to December, to 43.43 cents a kilowatt-hour including taxes. On 2 Oct it put September's gas price for 2.3 million vulnerable households 12.7% above August's, at a raw-material cost of 78.80 euros per MWh. That is 52% more than a year earlier, or about 1,782 euros a year for a typical home. On 16 Oct Brussels approved Rome's plan to cap the price of gas burned in power plants at roughly 58-59 euros per MWh, against a market near 85-90. That is worth about 10% off variable-rate power bills, but it starts only in 2027, after a decree due by year-end. In France, the regulator's benchmark home gas price rises 6.6% on 1 Nov (8.3% for heating), its third monthly rise in a row. Europe's wholesale gas price rose above 88 euros per MWh on 19 Oct, its highest since December 2022. It dipped to 85 on 20 Oct on reports of a US-Iran breakthrough and was back above 88 on 21 Oct. EU gas stores stood at 74.6% full against a 90% target.
developments.why_it_matters: The protests in Milan, Turin and Bologna are about the cost of living, and so far both governments' answers target diesel and riot damage: tax credits for Italian haulers, wages for staff at looted French shops. Heating and power bills are a separate household cost. Nothing announced so far softens them before 2027, and the heating season in northern Italy opened in mid-October.
developments.plain_summary: In Italy, power and gas bills are jumping just as the heating goes on. Households on the regulated power price pay 37% more for the last three months of the year, and their gas bill rose 13% in September alone. Europe's gas is at its highest since 2022 because Iran's war has cut off most of Qatar's gas. Rome won Brussels' approval to cap gas prices at power plants, but the cap does not start until 2027.
